item.title: Can a messy person change or are some people just naturally tidier?
item.description: Personality isn’t destiny and changing patterns may eventually change something about the kind of person we are.
item.content:encoded:
Some people seem naturally tidy. Their keys are always in the same place, clothes make it into the wardrobe, and their kitchen bench remains mysteriously visible.

Others can clean the house on Sunday and wonder by Wednesday how everything became messy again.

It’s tempting to explain this as personality: “I’m just a messy person.” And there is some truth to that. But personality isn’t destiny. Our surroundings and the small things we repeatedly do within them matter too.

In fact, changing those patterns may eventually change something about the kind of person we are.

Are some people just naturally tidier?

Psychologists describe personality in terms of relatively enduring patterns in how people tend to think, feel and behave.

One of the “Big Five” personality traits is conscientiousness. It includes tendencies towards being industrious, self-controlled and orderly. So, someone higher in conscientiousness – particularly its orderliness aspects – may find keeping things organised easier.

But “relatively enduring” doesn’t mean personality is fixed.

Large studies following people over time show personality is both stable and changeable. For example, people tend to become more conscientious during different stages of adulthood, such as when they have children or new responsibilities.

So, saying “I’m a messy person” may describe a tendency. It doesn’t condemn you to a lifetime of losing your keys.

item.title: How a love of gossip could make you a better reader
item.description: The intimacies and power dynamics navigated through a novel can be decoded by using the same skills we exercise when we gossip.
item.content:encoded:
In case you missed it, Rachel Cusk’s new novel Life of M has been the centre of heated online debate. Dubbed a “biogossip” (biography based on gossip) allegedly inspired by the actress Natalie Portman, the novel investigates fame, power and truth with a particular emphasis on storytelling.

Much of the discussion of the book revolves around the similarities between Portman’s real life rather than how Cusk explores her chosen themes. In a recent article for The Guardian, journalist Elle Hunt provides a handy list of must-know information for those wishing to read the novel but may be unsure of all the details. The biogossip argument is certainly plausible. For instance, references to Léon: The Professional (1994) and Black Swan (2010) are easy enough to pick up if you are aware of Portman’s filmography. At the conclusion, Hunt asks whether more gossip in literature could solve the crisis of people reading less than ever.

Sharing insider knowledge

It is interesting to consider whether easy-to-spot references to public figures are the key to drawing new readers in. However, asking for more gossip may be addressing the symptoms rather than the cause and ignores the fact that gossip has always existed in literature, and to a far greater extent than you might think.

item.title: These websites give you the thrill of online shopping without buying anything
item.description: A new trend emerging in South Korea allows users to browse products, place and order and even track its ‘delivery’.
item.content:encoded:
This article was originally published in Rest of World, which covers technology’s impact outside the West.

This week, I placed orders for a $44,860 Patek Philippe hand-engraved watch, a $12,500 Hermès handbag, a $9,800 Tiffany diamond ring, and a $7,350 Cartier Love bracelet in yellow gold.

I don’t need any of them. I certainly can’t afford them. Thankfully, they’ll never arrive.

Instead of Amazon, I spent the past week browsing a new breed of websites known as “dopamine sites,” a trend that emerged in South Korea. These websites – like Dopamine Shop and FoodNeverComes – recreate the entire ritual of online shopping: You search for products, compare reviews, add items to your cart, enter a shipping address, place an order, and even track your delivery.

Then … nothing happens. No money changes hands. No package arrives.

It’s tempting to dismiss them as another quirky internet trend. But after spending a week placing imaginary orders, I found myself wondering if online shopping has stopped being solely about buying things.

South Korea is one of the world’s most mature e-commerce markets, where digital payments, food delivery, and online retail are deeply embedded in everyday life. That makes it an ideal place for an idea like fake shopping to materialise. But the behaviour itself is far more...

item.title: Sunday book pick: Simone de Beauvoir’s ‘A Very Easy Death’ is a moving memoir about her dying mother
item.description: The memoir was originally published in French in 1964 as ‘Une Morte Très Douce.’ It was translated by Patrick O’Brian in 1965.
item.content:encoded:
“Her heart was in excellent condition and her blood pressure was that of a young woman: I had never been afraid of a sudden mishap for her.”

Simone de Beauvoir’s A Very Easy Death, a memoir about her dying mother, is the perfect read if you’re looking to fill a Mother Mary Comes to Me-sized hole in your heart.

An age to die

Beauvoir begins the story of her mother Françoise’s death with the news of her breaking the neck of her femur after a fall in the bathroom. Her neighbours call her daughters, Simone and Poupette, who immediately rush to the scene. Françoise is addressed as maman by her daughters and at 77, Beauvoir reasons that she is of an “age to die.” The hospital stay is longer than they expected, and the nurses help maman to eat, wash, and go to the bathroom. Beauvoir watches a swarm of people attending to her mother. Maman, who used to dress with consciousness, is made to wear nighties and is undressed several times a day as every nurse goes about her duty. Beauvoir is “jarred” by her mother’s nakedness, by how small and vulnerable she is.

The Keralam government on Sunday ordered a preliminary investigation into corruption allegations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar dating back 20 years, when he was the secretary of the state’s Public Works Department, The Hindu reported.

The development comes amid allegations against Kumar about irregularities in the conduct of the special intensive revision of voters rolls and calls from Opposition parties seeking his removal from office.

The Congress-led United Democratic Front government has directed the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau to probe allegations of bribery involving an Indo-Malaysian construction company that was awarded a contract to upgrade the Main Central Road under the Kerala State Transport Project. item.title: Raj Thackeray demands end to EVM voting, scrapping of Maharashtra SIR
item.description: Uddhav Thackeray accused Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of being ‘a weapon of the BJP’.
item.content:encoded:
Maharashtra Navnirman Sena chief Raj Thackeray on Sunday demanded that the special intensive revision of electoral rolls in Maharashtra be cancelled and that elections be conducted using ballot papers instead of electronic voting machines, citing alleged irregularities in the electoral process.

Speaking at a rally in Mumbai, Raj Thackeray questioned the deletion of voters through the SIR process, saying that two crore people had so far been removed and asking who those voters were.

“Who are these 2 crore people,” the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena chief asked. “When this matter is discussed in Delhi, I request all political parties to demand that SIR be canceled.”

The rally was jointly led by Raj Thackeray and his cousin, Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) chief Uddhav Thackeray. The march was held against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the SIR process, and was also attended by leaders of the Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar) and Congress.

Raj Thackeray quit the undivided Shiv Sena in 2005 and formed the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena a year later. The parties had been political rivals for the past two decades, but have in recent months come together.

item.title: ‘Termite’: Sirshendu Mukhopadhyay’s first novel tapped into urban alienation and existential drift
item.description: A new translation of the Bengali novel presents the protagonist’s acute indifference and his apparent lack of humane feelings.
item.content:encoded:
There are some novels that quietly unsettle you long after you’ve put them down. Ghunpoka, Bengali writer Sirshendu Mukhopadhyay’s first novel from the 1960s – now available in a new English translation as Termite – is certainly one of them. A haunting exploration of urban alienation and the modern existential drift, on its first publication the novel announced the arrival of a writer who would go on to reshape the Bengali literary landscape, turning away from conventional social realism towards a deep, inward, often unsettling focus on the uneasy terrain of the modern mind.

Calcutta, a psychological condition

Tapas Kumar Sen’s translation brings this early work to a contemporary readership with great care. In doing so, it also reintroduces a particular moment in Bengali literary history – when the city, especially Calcutta, began to be experienced not merely as a setting but as a psychological condition.

At the centre of the novel is Shyam, a young man who has drifted from the village of Banikhara in Bikrampur into the restless, indifferent sprawl of Calcutta. Despite a deep respect for his parents, Shyam represents a generation at odds with institutional authority. The number of voters in the state reduced to 71.5 lakh from 79.6 lakh before the exercise began, a decrease of about 10.1%.

Uttarakhand is among the 19 states and Union Territories where the voter roll revision is being carried out in the third phase of SIR.

On Saturday, Uttarakhand Chief Electoral Officer BVRC Purushottam said the final roll included 1.2 lakh newly enrolled voters, The Hindu reported.

item.title: How the Gujarati books of RF Sethna fed India’s appetite for books about Japan in the early 1900s
item.description: They were one of the many building blocks that helped Indians develop a better understanding of Japan and the Japanese.
item.content:encoded:
In his 1936 autobiography, Jawaharlal Nehru, the future prime minister of India, reccalls being deeply affected in his teenage years by the Russo-Japanese war of 1904-’05. “Japanese victories stirred up my enthusiasm and I waited eagerly for the papers for fresh news daily,” recounts Nehru, who 14 at the time. “I invested in a large number of books on Japan and tried to read some of them.”

It was the first time that the country of Japan had caught the attention of the Indian public. Japan had emerged from over two centuries of self-imposed isolation in the 1850s. Though trade between the two countries commenced soon thereafter, very few people in India knew anything about Japan, its society and its culture at the start of the twentieth century.

While Nehru could easily find books in English written by European and American authors, most Indians struggled to find books in their own languages. At a time when the printed word was the only source of information, the few books and articles on Japan that had been published in the nineteenth century seemed inadequate and out of date.

item.title: Why Opposition parties have not boycotted elections despite alleging polls are rigged
item.description: In their view, not contesting polls would amount to yielding space to the political forces they want to defeat.
item.content:encoded:
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party political campaign, on September 25 called on Opposition parties to boycott polls if they do not trust the Election Commission to hold free and fair polls.

Dipke contended that this was a logical inconsistency: why are they participating in exercises they contend are rigged? It is merely for their “political survival”, he claimed.

By participating in elections, Opposition parties help “maintain the illusion that they are free and fair”. But a boycott would deny Indian elections the legitimacy they now have, Dipke argued.

Dipke’s approach found support on social media. Among those who called for polls to be boycotted was former minister in the Narendra Modi Cabinet, RK Singh, who had resigned from the Bharatiya Janata party last year.

But even after several years of alleging irregularities in the electoral process, no Opposition party has so far given a serious thought to the idea of boycotting elections.

Some on social media defended Dipke’s approach, suggesting that boycotting elections would not mean merely sitting at home and doing nothing more. A boycott could result in new political movements being built, protests and mass mobilisation against the alleged irregularities in elections, they argued.

item.title: October Indian fiction: Bring in the festive season with these six new novels
item.description: A translation of a forgotten classic, the final novel in a sci-fi trilogy, a coming-of-age saga, and more.
item.content:encoded:
All information sourced from publishers.

All Our Evenings, Ruthvika Rao

In 1990s Hyderabad, three teenagers – Arjun, Ruhee and Ganesh – forge an unexpected bond. Over the course of a single sun-drenched summer, they discover love, friendship and solace from their troubled families. They also discover the Red House, an abandoned house in their neighbourhood, which becomes the site of their intimate friendship. But one night at the Red House, an unexpected act of violence shatters their lives forever.

A decade later, Ruhee returns to Hyderabad, and Arjun, who has never forgotten his first love, is given a chance to tell the truth, both to himself and to those around him. But the tangled threads of fate, class and desire remain, as does a lacerating secret.

item.title: Apple removes messaging app used by protesters to bypass internet restrictions in India
item.description: In July, youth protesters at Jantar Mantar relied on Bitchat to communicate after mobile internet was suspended in parts of central Delhi.
item.content:encoded:
Apple has removed the offline messaging application Bitchat from its India App Store after a demand from the Ministry of Information Technology, developer Jack Dorsey said on Saturday.

The removal came months after reports that youth demonstrators at Jantar Mantar, who were protesting against alleged irregularities in the conduct of competitive examinations, had been using such applications amid temporary internet restrictions that had been imposed at the protest site.

From Friday, protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over concerns about the functioning of the Election Commission and its handling of the special intensive revision of electoral rolls were held in Delhi and Mumbai.

Bitchat is an open-source, decentralised messaging application that allows nearby users to communicate without mobile data, Wi-Fi, phone numbers or centralised servers. It uses Bluetooth Low Energy to connect nearby phones, with each device capable of relaying messages to others and thereby extending the network’s reach. Private messages are end-to-end encrypted, and the application does not require users to create accounts or provide persistent identifiers.

While removal from the App Store does not delete Bitchat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates.

In July, the Union Home Ministry asked software platform GitHub to remove the repositories for Bitchat citing security concerns, according to a notice shared by Dorsey.

item.title: ‘Fusion cooking is an extension of imagination, memories, experiences’: Cookbook writer Rohini Rana
item.description: Rana is the author of ‘The Rana Cookbook’ and ‘Memories on a Platter’.
item.content:encoded:
Rohini Rana, affectionately known as Dolly, is a writer, culinary historian, and entrepreneur who is especially interested in preserving the rich culinary traditions of South Asia. She was born into the royal family of Awagarh in Uttar Pradesh and married into Nepal’s Rana family. Her travel, restaurant and social work, and her husband’s job in the army have deeply informed her writing.

Her books, The Rana Cookbook: Recipes from the Palaces of Nepal and The Nepal Cookbook: 108 Regional Recipes, documented royal and regional Nepali foodways with rare care and depth. Her latest book, Memories on a Platter: My Fusion Cookbook, brings together Indian, Nepali and global influences gathered through a life of movement, memory and hospitality, offering recipes that honour heritage while speaking to the modern palate.

Rana’s journey is a reminder that movement can also be a form of becoming. The book and author show us how food, memory and feminine resilience can exist gracefully on a platter. Her journey reminded me that a peripatetic life, one lived across postings, homes, cultures, kitchens and worlds, seasons a woman and makes her observant.

item.title: Ramachandra Guha: A century after Gandhi described the four pillars of swaraj, how do they hold up?
item.description: He pressed for equal rights for Dalits, women and minorities, an economic model that is equitable and sustainable, and the cultivation of non-violence.
item.content:encoded:
Mahatma Gandhi spent the last three decades of his life battling for his country’s freedom from British colonial rule. In this time, he rarely wrote or spoke about what he felt a free India should look like. However, in March 1922, he offered a short, succinct definition of swaraj that is worth revisiting today. Here is what he said:

“Removal of untouchability, manufacture of khaddar, Hindu-Muslim unity, cultivation of non-violence are not measures of a temporary nature. They are the four pillars on which the structure of swaraj must for ever rest. Take away any one of them and it must topple down.”

Let us unpack this statement and gloss each of its four elements.

We may take “removal of untouchability” to stand more broadly for the pursuit of social justice, which of course includes removing not just the inequalities of caste but also of gender. Unlike the other savarna leaders of the Congress – Nehru, Patel, Bose, et al – Gandhi was keenly aware of how the prevalence of untouchability undermined the Indian case for freedom. He therefore called it a “sin”, and those who practised it the “Dyers of Hinduism”.

item.title: Nigerian legend King Sunny Adé took African pop music to the world’s stage
item.description: The ‘King of Jùjú’ embodies an impressive blend of cultural grounding, musical innovation, entrepreneurial insight and global acclaim.
item.content:encoded:
Sunday Adeniyi Adegeye, known as King Sunny Adé, is 80 this year. He has devoted more than 60 years of his life to influencing Nigeria’s popular music and promoting the unique sounds of jùjú music.

Jùjú is a Nigerian musical tradition that combines intricate rhythms, percussion, guitars, talking drums, call-and-response and Yoruba oral culture. It’s not only entertainment but a vehicle for expressing cultural identity, transmitting proverbs and praise traditions, and social life commentary.

Sunny Adé’s career embodies an impressive blend of cultural grounding, musical innovation, entrepreneurial insight and global acclaim. From his beginnings in Lagos to his rise as the globally celebrated “King of Jùjú”, his story is intertwined with the development of contemporary African popular music.

As a social philosopher, I regard Sunny Adé’s music as a tool for social change. This is because it transforms cultural expression into a medium of moral reflection and social engagement. His music communicates values such as communal responsibility, respect, humility, peace, diligence and integrity. It also draws attention to the social problems confronting Nigerian society.

I’ve argued that Sunny Adé’s music addresses social challenges, preserves Yoruba identity and promotes civic awareness, national unity and moral renewal.

item.title: ‘Swan Song’: Princess Diana’s brother’s book is icy in its contempt for the British royal family
item.description: Charles Spencer casts King Charles, then the Prince of Wales, as a petulant child and ‘bellowing buffoon jealous of Diana’s star power’.
item.content:encoded:
Revenge is a dish best served cold, so the saying goes. Charles Spencer’s new memoir, Swan Song, arrives nearly three decades after his sister Diana’s death, and it is icy in its contempt for both the British tabloid media and the “arrogance and entitlement” of the royal family.

Dedicated to “all those who have lost a sibling”, and billed as revealing “the true framework of Diana’s life”, the memoir has been marketed as “the most intimate, loving and honest portrait” of Diana yet.

However, the book is as much about Spencer as it is about Diana. Over 350 pages, his litany of grievances swamps the loving tribute he ostensibly set out to write. King Charles, then the Prince of Wales, is cast as a petulant child and “bellowing buffoon” who was “always extremely jealous of Diana’s star power”.

Among the most damaging claims is that Charles was “giddily elated” on learning of Diana’s death, a reaction Spencer attributes to Charles’ “pent-up contempt for Diana and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death”, as well as what he sees as Charles’s relief at finally being free to marry the woman he loved.

item.title: Kolkata film institute suspends classes for sixth day after campus violence
item.description: Students are continuing their ‘academic boycott’, demanding the arrest of those responsible for injuring six of them on September 27.
item.content:encoded:
Classes at the Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute in Kolkata were suspended for the sixth day on Saturday as students continued their “academic boycott” over an alleged attack by members of a Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh-affiliated organisation on the campus, reported PTI.

The RSS, a Hindutva organisation, is the ideological parent of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

On September 27, at least six students were injured after being attacked for objecting to an event organised by members of the RSS-affiliated consumer group Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat.

The students’ union had stated that it was not informed about the event before the institute gave permission.

Poorvi Bondre, a member of the union, told Deutsche Welle that students confronted participants of the event after learning that the organisers were affiliated with the RSS and using the event to “promote its agenda” on campus.

“They called us anti-nationals and Naxals and attacked us with knives,” Bondre said.

Some students were also chased while others had their clothes torn and phones forcibly taken, the union had stated

Students have since been boycotting classes, demanding heightened security on campus and that those responsible for the violence be arrested, reported PTI.

item.title: ‘Love, fear, and a pursuit of fun’: What made Diksha Basu write a motherhood memoir
item.description: ‘This book began as my love letter to my daughters, and then it became a love letter to my mother.’
item.content:encoded:
I am a fiction writer. I find fiction safe, escapist, protective – a barrier against the world. It’s true, of course, that all fiction comes from reality and mine is no exception but I can always use an excuse with fiction when needed. When The Windfall was published, my mother insisted she saw my father on the pages and my father insisted he saw my mother on the pages. I quickly insisted neither of them was on the pages.

And now I sit on the eve of publishing my first longform nonfiction on one of the most vulnerable topics in the world – motherhood. And I have nowhere to hide. I find myself wondering why I wrote this book.

The now

Perhaps I wrote it out of self-defence. My daughters (currently eight and nine) and I do not yet have an emotionally complex relationship. The World Was Not Their Story: An Odyssey of an Indian Reporter, Saeed Naqvi

With few correspondents overseas, independent India’s newspapers have depended on agencies and publications in London or Washington, content to wear the blinkers of the West. item.title: How a British police officer turned his Indian postings into pulp fiction
item.description: Edmund Cox’s tales of detectives and dacoits, which drew on three decades of policing, revealed the prejudices and hierarchies of the colonial state.
item.content:encoded:
As his 30-year career in the British Indian police drew to a close, Edmund Cox found himself confounded by a wave of burglaries rippling through the Bombay suburb of Bandora, now Bandra. The houses being broken into belonged to wealthy families who had abandoned them during the plague of 1896-’97. For some time, the police had no idea who was responsible. Then, two thieves were caught in the act.

Their confession, Cox recalled, stunned the police. They were Waghris, members of what the colonial government called a “criminal tribe”. Scattered across the suburbs, they used the “Baroda railway” to slip in and out of the city at will, committing crimes with impunity.

It was precisely the sort of episode that stayed with Cox: a crime, a chase, a community already marked out by the police, and finally the satisfying moment when the mystery was solved. Years later, these experiences would become the raw material of his books.

Cox had spent much of his working life moving through the Bombay Presidency and beyond. item.title: SK Bole – the social reformer who mentored Ambedkar but then joined hands with Savarkar
item.description: He helped build the legal ground for the Mahad Satyagraha and ended his career as president of the Hindu Mahasabha.
item.content:encoded:
On 4 August 1924, Sitaram Keshav Bole moved a resolution in the Bombay Legislative Council granting untouchables access to public water bodies, wells, dharmashalas, schools, courts and hospitals. Three years later, it was this resolution that was invoked by BR Ambedkar, a lawyer who would go on to lead India’s Dalit rights movement, as he led thousands of so-called untouchables to Mahad to drink water from a public water tank that had been barred to them.

The Mahad satyagraha was a critical moment in the anti-caste movement – a movement whose young leader, Ambedkar, had been mentored by Bole since 1907.

Just over a decade later, in 1938, Bole – a man who had worked for decades on behalf of underprivileged castes and classes – became president of the Bombay Provincial Hindu Mahasabha, a Hindu nationalist organisation. This contradiction at the heart of Bole’s life has gone almost entirely unexamined.

Since branches were established in Maharashtra from 1923, the Hindu Mahasabha there had been dominated by Brahmins. Its politics centred on the challenges its leaders perceived from other religions, particularly Islam. Caste reform, the abolition of untouchability and the concerns of farmers and labourers were never part of its core agenda.

item.title: When does crowd control become ‘excessive’ police force?
item.description: India’s police manuals demand restraint and the bare minimum of force. So why do crackdowns from Jantar Mantar to Aarey Colony turn brutal?
item.content:encoded:
Among the questions the Supreme Court has asked the high-powered enquiry committee to answer on the Cockroach Janata Party protest crackdown, one has received more attention than others: did the police use “excessive force and violence” against protesters at Jantar Mantar on July 20?

The question undoubtedly merits attention. Going by the accounts of the petitioners, witnesses and human rights bodies, the clampdown was ferocious. Apart from batons and tear gas, the police allegedly used nail-studded lathis, rubber bullets, electric batons and even pellet guns. A Human Rights Watch report quotes a 24-year-old photojournalist as saying, “I have photos of protesters just standing there and the police beating them.”

But beyond the specifics of the protest at Jantar Mantar, there is another question in the Supreme Court order raised by the petitioners. What is “a proportionate and measured police response” to protests and peaceful assemblies that strikes an “appropriate balance between the maintenance of public order and the constitutional right to peaceful dissent”?

It is not hard to see the inherent conflict between the two mandates. Article 19(1)(b) of the Indian Constitution guarantees all citizens the right to assemble peaceably without arms, while Article 19(3) places restrictions on this very freedom in the interest of public order and the sovereignty and integrity of the country.

item.title: Nutrients in food mimic calorie restrictions. Can they improve our health?
item.description: Research in humans has yet to show that compounds reproduce the effects of calorie restriction or extend healthspan.
item.content:encoded:
Scroll through social media and you will soon encounter advice about living longer, from fasting plans and supplements to elaborate daily routines. Yet reaching an advanced age tells us little about how healthy or independent those later years will be.

Researchers often use the term healthspan for the years spent in good health, free from disability or chronic disease. In 2021, global life expectancy was 71.4 years, while healthy life expectancy was 61.9 years, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). That represents a gap of nine and a half years. A separate analysis estimated that this gap widened in 203 of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.

The WHO takes a broader view of healthy ageing, focusing on the abilities that allow people to do what they value, such as undertaking daily tasks, maintaining relationships and contributing to society. This recognises that people can live well while managing a health condition. “Functional healthspan” describes how long someone maintains the capacities needed for independent living.

As we age, declining muscle strength and mass, reduced aerobic fitness and even “inflammaging” (or low-grade inflammation) become more prevalent. These changes vary considerably between people. Diet, physical activity and sleep can influence how well we age, although income, housing, healthcare and the wider environment also play important roles.

item.title: How ‘new’ is the tilcayo, the first cat species to be discovered in a 100 years?
item.description: Researchers knew of a tiger cat occurred in Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forests, but it had never been formally described.
item.content:encoded:
Scientists have described a species of tiger cat that was previously unknown to science. From Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forests, it is the first discovery of a living novel cat species in more than 100 years.

The tilcayo (Leopardus tilcayo) takes its species name from the name locals already had for it. Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer who discovered the species and co-author of the Current Biology paper that describes it, said the name honors traditional knowledge in the region.

The tilcayo is smaller than a domestic cat at 1.4 kilograms (3 pounds). It has rounded ears, a slender body and a coat with large spots.

“I have the honor of naming a cat, and that’s a really big thing,” Nogales-Ascarrunz, who is also a researcher at the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz, Bolivia, told Mongabay by phone.

For decades, researchers lumped small spotted cats across South America under a single species name: Leopardus tigrinus or tiger cat. However, evidence had been mounting for years that the group might contain several species.

In the article published on September 17, researchers unwound the species’ genetic web and confirmed at least four distinct species.

item.title: From Azad Hind Radio to Gandhi: The forgotten Indian story of Surinamese composer Majoie Hajary
item.description: The pianist with Indian roots moved from wartime radio and New Delhi to ragas, devotional music and one of the most unusual Gandhi recordings of the 1960s.
item.content:encoded:
Any serious conversation about Gandhi and music would be incomplete without discussing a French record from 1968. Requiem pour Mahatma Gandhi was composed by Majoie Hajary, who was born in Suriname, trained in Amsterdam and Paris, spent time in New Delhi and moved throughout her life between musical worlds that others had preferred to keep apart.

Hajary was born in 1921 in Paramaribo, capital of the Dutch colony of Suriname in South America. While her father was born in Suriname, her paternal grandparents had come from India. Her mother was Afro-Chinese. Her ancestors had come to the colony as indentured labourers.

Hajary grew up in comfort, principally with Western classical music at home.

Ellen de Vries, author of the 2025 Hajary biography Surinaamse Rapsodie and the researcher behind a website about the composer, majoiehajary.org, helped fill in some of the gaps in Hajary’s Indian story.

In an email message, de Vries said that 15-year-old Hajary left for Amsterdam in 1937 to study at the conservatory, already carrying more than one musical language with her. Her interest in Indian music deepened in the Dutch capital, and later through encounters with Indian musicians and teachers in Berlin in Germany and Caracas in Venezuela.

item.title: The start of a run can feel like a fight against your body – and that is normal
item.description: This sensation is actually caused by a normal feature of human physiology.
item.content:encoded:
Many runners describe the first ten to 15 minutes of a run as the hardest of all. Breathing can feel laboured, the legs can feel heavy and a pace that would normally seem manageable may suddenly feel surprisingly difficult.

It might be easy to assume the reason your run feels so difficult at the start is because you’re not fit enough. But in reality, this sensation is actually caused by a normal feature of human physiology – and one that affects almost everyone, from someone attempting their first 5K to elite endurance athletes.

One way I often explain this phenomenon to athletes and students is that when you begin running, an argument starts between your muscles and your cardiorespiratory system. While there’s nothing we can do to stop this quarrel from happening, there are many things we can do to help the body find a resolution more quickly in the future.

The moment you start running, your working muscles demand a rapid supply of energy almost instantly. Yet the system responsible for producing that energy from oxygen cannot respond quite as quickly.

item.title: As India’s exotic pet trade flourishes, abandonment of animals is an ecological danger
item.description: Removing animals from native ecosystems affects the ecological functions they perform while introducing them into new territories can alter the environment.
item.content:encoded:
India’s exotic pet trade has grown from a niche pursuit into a significant industry. Over 40,000 people across 30 states and union territories declared their exotic pets in the government’s 2020 Voluntary Disclosure Scheme, making the scale of ownership hard to ignore, according to a Humane World for Animals report published this year. For Tyeb Mehta, the line was never merely a formal device. It carried philosophical and emotional weight, embodying memory, myth, pain and redemption, with an intensity that was both provocative and contemplative. It is through his drawings that we trace the paradox at the heart of his practice: that the instability we perceive on his canvases was carefully engineered.

Mehta’s drawings have piqued visitors to the retrospective Tyeb Mehta: Bearing Weight (with the lightness of being). Largely unseen for decades, they facilitate fresh curatorial perspectives on his visual language. We seldom see an artist’s preliminary exercises or the evolutionary charting of a creative practice. In 2019, The Gambia filed an application at the ICJ alleging that Myanmar had violated the United Nations’ 1948 Genocide Convention in its treatment of the Rohingya people.

The Rohingya are an ethnic minority group that have long lived in the Arakan region of western Myanmar, which today corresponds to the Rakhine state.

item.title: ‘Major food crisis’ likely in coming months amid West Asia and Russia wars, warns S Jaishankar
item.description: The conflicts have caused fertiliser shortages and disruptions in grain shipments, which have been ‘very stressful’ for the Global South, he said.
item.content:encoded:
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has warned that there may be a “major food crisis” in the coming months amid fertiliser shortages and disruptions in grain shipments caused by the wars in Ukraine and West Asia.

On top of it, “there’s the super El Niño”, said Jaishankar while speaking at an event hosted at Asia Society in New York on Monday.

The El Niño phenomenon involves the warming of ocean surface temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific. It typically occurs every few years and has been linked to crop damage, fires and flash floods.

On Tuesday, the Union government revised its food grain production target to 373.9 million tonnes for 2026-’27, which is 2.6 million tonnes lower than the estimated output in 2025-’26, reported The Indian Express. The decision was taken in view of the situation created by El Niño, said Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan.

Additionally, India’s fertiliser industry is reeling under the disruption in energy supplies from West Asia amid the conflict there. The industry depends heavily on liquefied natural gas imported from the region as raw material to manufacture fertilisers domestically.
